<reason>Both sides argued competently, but B built a tighter, more consistent throughline (the sale itself, not the money, is the harm; it is irrevocable and exports risk to 26 states) and used the pressure round to extract real concessions. A's answer to B's Q1 never named a surviving citizenship-by-investment program and instead reframed the question, which B correctly flagged in closing as a half-concession of the motion. A's strongest structural argument—that killing legal channels pushes buyers into shadow methods—was blunted by B's distinction that those alternatives are prosecutable crimes while a purchased passport is legal and permanent. Most damaging, B's "convergence" argument (that CON's own reformed model strips out every feature that makes the program a sale, leaving only an ordinary entrepreneur visa) went largely unanswered in A's closing, which could only assert that "branding shouldn't matter" without explaining what distinctive, defensible thing remains. B's clipped Rebuttal 1 is a real execution cost, but the loss was a single trailing sentence and did not blunt B's overall trajectory or its command of the later rounds.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's closing move—turning CON's own "reformed" program description into an admission that nothing sale-specific survives except "pay, skip the queue, receive the document"—was the most decisive exchange; A's closing could not rebut it beyond calling it "branding."</best_rebuttal>
